page4_img_2.png.title: Developers vs Reporters: which bug-report details are most helpful
page4_img_2.png.description: A side-by-side ranked list comparing what developers say is most useful in bug reports (left) versus what reporters believe they provide (right), with lines linking corresponding items. Both groups top-rank “steps to reproduce” (developers 83%, reporters 78%), but developers report higher need for stack traces (57%) and test cases (51%) than reporters say they supply (stack traces 33%, test cases 43%). Another notable gap is screenshots: 26% of developers find them helpful while only 5% of reporters provide them. The diagram shows overall agreement in rank order but highlights systematic under-provision of several items developers consider important (stack traces, screenshots, code examples).

page2_img_2.png.title: Socio-technical network linking developers and modules
page2_img_2.png.description: A schematic socio-technical graph showing modules (green/blue circles labeled A–G) and developers (pink rounded boxes labeled Fred and Ram). Solid directed edges between circles represent technical module dependencies (A↔B/C and many small arrows around D/E/F/G indicating other dependency connections), while dashed lines connect developers to modules to indicate contribution relationships (Fred linked to D and E and Ram linked to F and G, both also dashed-linked to central module A). The diagram emphasizes a central module (A) that is both technically connected to other modules and touched by multiple developers, illustrating how the paper combines contribution and dependency edges into one graph to improve prediction of failure-prone modules.

page2_img_1.png.title: Commit-weighted developer–module contribution network
page2_img_1.png.description: A small developer–module bipartite graph where circles are developers and squares are modules; numeric labels on edges are commit counts (edge weights). Module “b” (left square) is connected to Eric (5), Fu (6), Dan (4) and Bob (2); module “a” (right square) is connected to Alice (6), Bob (4), Go (2) and Hin (5). A third module “c” is partially shown below/right, connected from Go (7) and Hin (4). The figure highlights developers (Bob, Hin) who contribute to multiple modules and thus act as cross-module connectors — a topological property the paper uses (centrality and commit counts) to predict post-release faults.

page7_img_1.png.title: World map of ESE group locations and collaborators
page7_img_1.png.description: A muted Bing world map showing the geographic footprint of the Empirical Software Engineering (ESE) group and its collaborators. Two black pin markers indicate the ESE group’s main locations (Redmond, USA and Cambridge, UK), while orange star markers show collaborating Microsoft labs, interns and visitors distributed across North America, Europe and Asia. Labeled in the paper as collaborator sites are Microsoft Research India (Bangalore), Microsoft Research Asia (Beijing) and the European Microsoft Innovation Center (Aachen); the authors also note intern and visitor affiliations (e.g., University of Virginia, UC Santa Cruz, Stanford, Boğaziçi University, Darmstadt, NC State, NIT Tiruchirappalli), which correspond to other orange markers on the map. The figure visualizes the group’s global collaborations and the concentration of activity in the US, western Europe, India and China.

page4_img_1.png.title: Developer vs. reporter bug-report information comparison
page4_img_1.png.description: Two vertical lists compare what developers consider most helpful in a bug report (left) with what reporters say they provide (right), with connecting lines mapping corresponding items. The left column shows items and developer percentages: steps to reproduce (83%), stack traces (57%), test cases (51%), observed behavior (33%), screenshots (26%), expected behavior (22%), code examples (14%), summary (13%), version (12%), error reports (12%), build information (8%), product (5%), operating system (4%), component (3%), hardware (0%), severity (0%). The right column shows reporter self-reported provision rates: steps to reproduce (98%), observed behavior (96%), expected behavior (94%), product (94%), version (91%), operating system (90%), summary (90%), component (87%), severity (77%), build information (60%), screenshots (60%), test cases (56%), error reports (53%), stack traces (50%), hardware (48%), code examples (36%). The figure highlights a mismatch: reporters claim to provide many high-level contextual fields at high rates, while developers emphasize technical artifacts (stack traces, test cases) that reporters report less frequently, as indicated by the connection lines and differing percentages.
